synopsis: The fatality evidence points beyond object collisions: of 54 US haul-truck deaths in January 2005–June 2021, 21 involved berms, 12 dump points, 13 collisions with people or vehicles, and eight other causes; 12 of the 13 collision deaths involved forward movement [f2989, f2990]. Unintended braking can itself create serious hazards, including load shift, loss of traction, rollover or instability, and rear-end impacts from following trucks; shadow mode cannot establish whether a false stop causes such a collision [f1129, f8201, f596]. Sensor validation must address substantial blind areas and occlusion: a 50 t truck's front-right blind area extends at least 18 m, while a 2026 mine study reported only 5.0% lidar visible-region recovery for an occluded truck [f11403, f4357]. The evidence base remains limited: the 2022 NIOSH review found detection-reliability testing in only 13 of 99 metric instances, avoidance or intervention systems in only 10% of 97 cases, and only 8% of articles above technology readiness level 7; the booklet still identifies the 2006 radar study as its best hard false-alarm source [f5170, f5171, f5172, f5173]. December 2021 Wabtec tests demonstrated controlled deceleration up to 30 km/h but still required physical detection-zone adjustment, while modern machine-delay distributions and site reconstruction studies at large-machine sensor heights of 3–6 m were not found [f1345, f1247, f5899, f4382]. Validation also needs to cover operational failures rather than perception alone: 2019 autonomous-haulage collisions implicated communications and traction, and a WorkSafe WA report dated 7 March 2025 records trucks resuming movement after communications returned while operators misunderstood their mode; transferring on-road evidence to loaded haul trucks on gravel remains an open question [f1371, f10718, f11349].
